765-KV TRANSMISSION LINE PROJECT                                        §                  HEARINGS
IN BELL, BURNET, CONCHO, CORYELL,                                       §
LAMPASAS, LLANO, MASON,                                                 §
McCULLOCH, MENARD, MILAM, MILLS,                                        §
SAN SABA, SCHLEICHER, TOM GREEN,                                        §
AND WILLIAMSON COUNTIES                                                 §

                         INITIAL BRIEF OF INTERVENORS
                    BENJAMIN FRIOU AND ELIZABETH ANN FRIOU

       Intervenors Benjamin Friou and Elizabeth Ann Friou (“the Frious”) submit this Initial
Brief. The Frious own real property located at 2100 County Road 209, Florence, Williamson
County, Texas, that will be affected by the proposed transmission line. This Brief is based on the
Frious’ direct testimony and opposes any route using segments F43 or G43, the southernmost route
segment identified in Figure 3 of the applicants’ transmission-line map.

       This Initial Brief identifies each of the issues in the Order of Referral and the Preliminary
Order, although the Frious have no comment on several of the issues. The Frious do not, in this
Brief, contest the overall need for the project; they confine their position to the routing of the F43
to G43 segment, which crosses federally protected endangered-species habitat, is longer and more
costly than necessary, and parallels an existing transmission corridor.

                                                  SUMMARY
   •   The Frious own property at 2100 County Road 209, Florence, Williamson County, Texas,
       that is directly affected by the proposed F43 to G43 segment. The Frious oppose any
       route using segments F43 or G43.




                  Initial Brief of Intervenors Benjamin Friou and Elizabeth Ann Friou   Page 1 of 11
 •   The F43 to G43 route crosses Cobbs Springs and Cobb Springs Branch in Williamson
    County, which provide habitat for the federally endangered Salado Salamander (Eurycea
    chisholmensis, the population formerly listed as the Georgetown Salamander, Eurycea
    naufragia) and the federally endangered Jollyville Plateau salamander (Eurycea
    tonkawae). Cobbs Springs lies within U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service designated critical
    habitat Unit 6 for the Salado Salamander.

•   These are fully aquatic, groundwater-dependent species with no tolerance for water
    pollution, groundwater disruption, or habitat degradation. Construction of a 765-kV line
    across this location, including tower-foundation drilling in karst limestone, is
    incompatible with the continued survival of the populations there.

•   The applicants have not properly coordinated with the Texas Parks and Wildlife
    Department, and the record documents no consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife
    Service under Section 7 of the Endangered Species Act, as required. The applicants have
    not addressed the route’s impact on these endangered species or on designated critical
    habitat Unit 6. That omission is a material deficiency.

•   The F43 to G43 segment is not the most direct route between the relevant endpoints and
    is therefore probably not the most cost-effective, imposing higher construction, materials,
    and operation-and-maintenance costs on Texas ratepayers.

•   The F43 to G43 route runs very close and nearly parallel to an existing transmission
    corridor. The applicants have not explained why the existing corridor is inadequate or
    why a new parallel right-of-way, condemning new private land, is necessary.

•   The route would diminish the value of the Frious’ entire parcel, consistent with the jury’s
    finding in Oncor Electric Delivery Co. v. Clack.

•   The Commission should decline to approve any route using segments F43 or G43 until
    the applicants cure these deficiencies.

                     ISSUES FROM THE ORDER OF REFERRAL

Joint Application




              Initial Brief of Intervenors Benjamin Friou and Elizabeth Ann Friou   Page 2 of 11
    •   Is the applicants’ joint application to amend its CCN adequate? Does the application
       contain an adequate number of reasonably differentiated alternative routes to conduct a
       proper evaluation?

The application is not adequate as to the southernmost F43 to G43 segment. The applicants bear
the burden under PURA § 37.056(c) of demonstrating that the route they selected is necessary and
appropriate. The application, however, does not justify the selection of a longer, less direct, and
more expensive southernmost route; does not explain why a new parallel right-of-way is needed
alongside an existing corridor; and does not address the route’s impact on the federally endangered
Salado Salamander and Jollyville Plateau salamander or on designated critical habitat Unit 6. To
the Frious’ knowledge, the applicants’ filings do not contain that justification.

   Notice
   •   Did the applicant provide notice of the application in accordance with 16 TAC §
       22.52(a)(1), (2), and (3), and notice of the public meeting in accordance with 16 TAC §
       22.52(a)(4)?

The Frious have no comment.

   Public Input
   •   What were the principal concerns expressed in the questionnaire responses received at or
       after any public meetings held by the applicants regarding the proposed transmission
       facilities?

The Frious, as directly affected landowners, oppose any route using segments F43 or G43 for the
reasons set out in this Brief: the crossing of federally endangered salamander habitat at Cobbs
Springs, the longer and more costly southernmost routing, the unnecessary condemnation of new
land parallel to an existing corridor, and the diminution of property value.

   Need
   •   Taking into account the factors set out in PURA § 37.056(c), are the proposed
       transmission facilities necessary for the service, accommodation, convenience, or safety
       of the public, and what is the historical and forecasted load and the better-option
       analysis under PURA § 37.056(c)(2)?




                     Initial Brief of Intervenors Benjamin Friou and Elizabeth Ann Friou   Page 3 of 11
 The Frious take no position on the overall need for the project and confine this Brief to the routing
of the F43 to G43 segment.

   Route
   •   Weighing the factors set forth in PURA § 37.056(c) and 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B), which
       proposed transmission-line route is the best alternative?

The F43 to G43 segment is not the best alternative and should not be approved. Three independent
routing defects, each weighed by the statutory criteria, disqualify it, and a fourth concern, property-
value diminution, weighs further against it.

First defect: environmental integrity and federally endangered species.
The F43 to G43 route crosses Cobbs Springs and Cobb Springs Branch in Williamson County.
Cobbs Springs provides habitat for the federally endangered Salado Salamander, Eurycea
chisholmensis. That population was previously listed as the Georgetown Salamander, Eurycea
naufragia; subsequent genetic analysis reclassified it as the Salado Salamander, which is also
federally listed as endangered and has a distribution across Williamson and Bell Counties, Texas.
Cobb Springs Branch also provides habitat for the federally endangered Jollyville Plateau
salamander, Eurycea tonkawae, a small, fully aquatic species found exclusively in springs and wet
caves within the Brushy Creek and Bull Creek watersheds in Travis and Williamson Counties.

Each species is neotenic and fully aquatic, retaining its external gills for life and inhabiting the
water column under rocks and within gravel in spring outflows and spring-fed streams and caves.
Each depends entirely on a high-quality, stable, clean, cold, well-oxygenated, groundwater-fed
environment, and has no tolerance for water pollution, groundwater disruption, or habitat
degradation, which accounts for the federally endangered status of each under the Endangered
Species Act.

The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service has designated critical habitat for the Salado Salamander, and
Cobbs Springs is located within proposed critical habitat Unit 6. The Service has specifically
evaluated this location and concluded that Cobbs Springs and the adjacent Cobbs Well constitute
the same population within a subsurface habitat area of approximately 300 meters. Any federal
nexus associated with this project triggers a consultation obligation under Section 7 of the
Endangered Species Act, both as to the listed species and as to that designated critical habitat.


                  Initial Brief of Intervenors Benjamin Friou and Elizabeth Ann Friou   Page 4 of 11
 Construction of a 765-kV transmission line crossing Cobbs Springs poses direct and material risks
to these species. Tower-foundation drilling in karst limestone terrain, the geology characteristic of
this area, can fracture subsurface rock and alter the groundwater flow paths that feed the springs.
Construction activities introduce sediment, fuel, and other contaminants into what must remain
pristine spring water. Right-of-way clearing removes the riparian vegetation that moderates water
temperature and water quality in the stream. And the long-term presence of the transmission line
creates a permanent corridor for maintenance activities that will repeatedly disturb this sensitive
habitat.

Benjamin Friou served as a field monitor for salamanders at Cobbs Springs and is familiar with
the precise habitat conditions there. In his judgment, routing a 765-kV transmission line across
this location is incompatible with the continued survival of the salamander population there. The
Commission is required under PURA § 37.056(c) to consider environmental integrity in its
evaluation. The applicants have not, to the Frious’ knowledge, addressed the impact of the F43 to
G43 route on the Salado Salamander, on the Jollyville Plateau salamander, on designated critical
habitat Unit 6, or on Cobbs Springs and Cobb Springs Branch. That omission is a material
deficiency that must be corrected before any route approval.

Second defect: a longer, less direct route.
The F43 to G43 segment, the southernmost route proposed in this proceeding, is not the most direct
route between the relevant transmission endpoints and is therefore probably not the most cost-
effective routing option. This defect bears on both the routing criteria and the cost to consumers
addressed below.

Third defect: an unnecessary parallel corridor.
The F43 to G43 route runs very close and nearly parallel to an existing transmission-line corridor.
Sound infrastructure planning and basic principles of land stewardship weigh strongly against
condemning new private land for a new parallel corridor when an existing corridor may serve the
same purpose. Using an existing right-of-way avoids the condemnation of additional private land,
reduces the total footprint of transmission infrastructure on the landscape, minimizes the number
of landowners affected, avoids the need for environmental review of a previously undisturbed
corridor, including the endangered-species crossing, and eliminates the additional costs of
acquiring a new right-of-way. The applicants have not explained why the existing adjacent corridor


                   Initial Brief of Intervenors Benjamin Friou and Elizabeth Ann Friou   Page 5 of 11
 is inadequate and why a new parallel right-of-way is necessary, and that explanation is part of their
burden of proof under PURA § 37.056(c).

Community values and property value.
The Commission is required under PURA § 37.056(c) to consider community values, historical
and aesthetic values, and the effect of the proposed line on landowners and the surrounding area.
The presence of a 765-kV transmission line on or adjacent to a property has well-documented
effects on property value, including the stigma associated with large high-voltage infrastructure,
the loss of scenic and aesthetic value, viewshed impacts from 200-foot steel lattice towers, and the
land-use restrictions imposed by the right-of-way itself. In Oncor Electric Delivery Co. v. Clack,
a Wichita County jury awarded a landowner approximately eight times Oncor’s initial
condemnation offer for a 345-kV line because the jury found the transmission infrastructure
diminished the value of the entire parcel, not merely the strip of land within the right-of-way. The
lines proposed here are 765-kV, with significantly larger towers, wider rights-of-way, greater
EMF, and far greater documented health, safety, and environmental impacts than the 345-kV line
at issue in Clack, so the property-value harm can reasonably be expected to exceed what the jury
recognized there.

   •   Are there alternative routes or configurations of facilities that would have a less negative
       effect on landowners, and what would be the incremental cost of those routes or
       configurations?

Yes. A more direct alternative routing between the same endpoints, and the use of the existing
adjacent corridor, would each have a less negative effect on landowners and the environment than
the F43 to G43 segment, and would avoid the endangered-species crossing at Cobbs Springs
entirely. As to incremental cost, the comparison runs in the Frious’ favor: because the F43 to G43
segment is the longer, less direct, and more expensive option, the alternatives reduce cost rather
than add it. The applicants, who bear the burden, have not quantified or justified the difference,
and have not demonstrated that the southernmost route is necessary and appropriate.

           ◦   Have the affected landowners made adequate contributions to offset any
               additional costs associated with the accommodations, and have the
               accommodations diminished the electric efficiency of the line or reliability?



                    Initial Brief of Intervenors Benjamin Friou and Elizabeth Ann Friou   Page 6 of 11
 The Frious have no comment on these sub-issues.

   Cost to Consumers
   •   Are the proposed transmission facilities necessary to meet state or federal reliability
       standards?

The Frious have no comment.

   •   What is the estimated cost of the proposed transmission facilities to consumers?

As to the F43 to G43 segment specifically, the route is not the most direct between the relevant
endpoints and is therefore probably not the most cost-effective. A route that is longer than
necessary imposes higher construction costs, higher materials costs, and higher ongoing operation-
and-maintenance costs over the life of the asset, all of which are ultimately borne by the Texas
ratepayers who will fund this infrastructure for a generation or more. The burden of demonstrating
that the selected route is necessary and appropriate falls squarely on the applicants, and to the
extent a more direct and less costly alternative exists between the same endpoints, the applicants
should be required to justify their selection of the longer, less direct, and more expensive
southernmost route. The applicants should also account for the property-value diminution
discussed above, which is an additional cost the F43 to G43 route imposes on affected landowners.

   •   What is the estimated congestion cost savings for consumers that may result from the
       proposed transmission facilities?

The Frious have no comment.

   Best Management Practices
   •   Are the standard best management practices adequate? If not, what additional practices
       should be required for the proposed transmission facilities?

For the F43 to G43 crossing of Cobbs Springs and Cobb Springs Branch, no standard construction
or operating best management practice can render the route compatible with the survival of the
endangered salamander populations, because the harms (fracturing of karst limestone, alteration
of the groundwater flow paths that feed the springs, contamination of pristine spring water,
removal of riparian vegetation, and recurring maintenance disturbance) flow from the construction
and permanent presence of the line itself. The appropriate practice is avoidance: route away from



                 Initial Brief of Intervenors Benjamin Friou and Elizabeth Ann Friou   Page 7 of 11
 segments F43 and G43, and, at a minimum, complete coordination with the Texas Parks and
Wildlife Department and consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service under Section 7 of
the Endangered Species Act before any route decision affecting this habitat.

    Texas Parks and Wildlife Department
    •   Did the Texas Parks and Wildlife Department provide any recommendations or
        informational comments regarding this application in accordance with section
        12.0011(b) of the Texas Parks and Wildlife Code, and if so, how should the Commission
        respond through its order?

The dispositive point for the Frious is that the applicants did not properly coordinate with the Texas
Parks and Wildlife Department as required. A complete CCN application and a proper
environmental routing analysis require the applicants to coordinate with the Department, to request
its recommendations and informational comments under Texas Parks and Wildlife Code §
12.0011(b), and to document and address that coordination in the environmental assessment
supporting the application. To the Frious’ knowledge, the record contains no evidence that the
applicants coordinated with the Department regarding the F43 to G43 segment’s crossing of Cobbs
Springs and Cobb Springs Branch, the federally endangered Salado Salamander and Jollyville
Plateau salamander, or the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service’s designated critical habitat Unit 6. Nor
does the record document the consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service that Section 7
of the Endangered Species Act requires where a federal nexus exists.

That failure to coordinate goes to the heart of the environmental-integrity criterion under PURA §
37.056(c) and 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B), and it is a material deficiency in the application. The
Commission should respond through its order by, first, requiring the applicants to coordinate with
the Texas Parks and Wildlife Department and to place the Department’s recommendations and
informational comments in the record; second, requiring the applicants to document any
consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service under Section 7 of the Endangered Species
Act, both as to the listed species and as to designated critical habitat Unit 6; and third, declining to
approve any route using segments F43 or G43 until that coordination and consultation are complete
and have been scrutinized in this proceeding.

    Permits



                  Initial Brief of Intervenors Benjamin Friou and Elizabeth Ann Friou   Page 8 of 11
    •   What permits, licenses, plans, or permission will be required for construction and
       operation of the proposed transmission facilities?

At minimum, the F43 to G43 route implicates consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service
under Section 7 of the Endangered Species Act, and may require additional federal authorization,
with respect to the federally endangered Salado Salamander and Jollyville Plateau salamander and
the designated critical habitat at Cobbs Springs. The applicants have not shown that they have
obtained, or even initiated, the necessary wildlife-agency coordination and consultation, and the
Commission should require proof of these permissions before approving the segment.

   Coastal Management Program
   •   Is any part of the proposed transmission facilities located within the coastal management
       program boundary as defined in 31 TAC § 27.1(a)?

The Frious have no comment.

   Limitation of Authority
   •   Are the circumstances for this line such that the seven-year limit discussed in section VI
       of the Order should be changed?

The Frious have no comment.

   Other Issues
   •   Will anything occur during construction that will preclude or limit a generator from
       generating or delivering power or that will adversely affect the reliability of the ERCOT
       system?

The Frious have no comment.

   •   If complete or partial agreement of the parties is reached on a route that relies on
       modifications to the route segments as noticed in the application, please address the
       associated issues.

The Frious have reached no agreement and oppose any route using segments F43 or G43. The
Frious do not oppose a route that avoids those segments, uses the existing adjacent corridor, and
avoids the Cobbs Springs salamander habitat.




                  Initial Brief of Intervenors Benjamin Friou and Elizabeth Ann Friou   Page 9 of 11
                                                CONCLUSION
For the reasons stated, the Frious respectfully request that the Commission decline to approve any
route using segments F43 or G43, and require the applicants to address the following before
approving the F43 to G43 route segment:

   •   Submit a full analysis of the impact of the F43 to G43 route on the federally endangered
       Salado Salamander (Eurycea chisholmensis) and the Jollyville Plateau salamander
       (Eurycea tonkawae) and their habitat at Cobbs Springs and Cobb Springs Branch,
       including documentation of coordination with the Texas Parks and Wildlife Department
       and of any consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service under Section 7 of the
       Endangered Species Act, and as to designated critical habitat Unit 6.

   •   Demonstrate, with route-specific analysis, that the F43 to G43 route is more direct and
       more cost-effective than available alternative routes between the same endpoints, or
       select and justify a more appropriate route.

   •   Demonstrate why the existing adjacent transmission corridor is technically inadequate for
       the proposed transmission purpose before condemning new private land for a parallel
       right-of-way.

   •   Address the property-value impacts of the F43 to G43 route on affected landowners,
       consistent with the Commission’s obligations under PURA § 37.056(c).

Because the applicants have not properly coordinated with the Texas Parks and Wildlife
Department, have not documented the required consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife
Service, and have not addressed the route’s impact on the endangered salamander species and their
designated critical habitat, the Commission should decline to approve any route using segments
F43 or G43.

                                                     SCHEEF & STONE, L.L.P.

this location is incompatible with the continued survival of the salamander population there. The
Commission is required under PLJRA § 37.056(c) to consider environmental integrity in its
evaluation. The applicants have not, to the Frious' knowledge, addressed the impact of the F43 to
G43 route on the Salado Salamander, on the Jollyville Plateau salamander, on designated critical
habitat Unit 6, or on Cobbs Springs and Cobb Springs Branch. That omission is a material
deficiency that must be corrected before any route approval.

Second defect: a longer, less direct route.
The F43 to G43 segment, the southernmost route proposed in this proceeding, is not the most direct
route between the relevant transmission endpoints and is therefore probably not the most cost-
effective routing option. This defect bears on both the routing criteria and the cost to consumers
addressed below.

Third defect: an unnecessary parallel corridor.
The F43 to G43 route runs very close and nearly parallel to an existing transmission-line corridor.
Sound infrastructure planning and basic principles of land stewardship weigh strongly against
condemning new private land for a new parallel corridor when an existing corridor may serve the
same purpose. Using an existing right-of-way avoids the condemnation of additional private land,
reduces the total footprint of transmission infrastructure on the landscape, minimizes the number
of landowners affected, avoids the need for environmental review of a previously undisturbed
corridor, including the endangered-species crossing, and eliminates the additional costs of
acquiring a new right-of-way. The applicants have not explained why the existing adjacent corridor

 is inadequate and why a new parallel right-of-way is necessary, and that explanation is part oftheir
burden of proof under PURA § 37.056(c)

Community values and property value.
The Commission is required under PURA § 37.056(c) to consider community values, historical
and aesthetic values, and the effect of the proposed line on landowners and the surrounding area.
The presence of a 765-kV transmission line on or adjacent to a property has well-documented
effects on property value, including the stigma associated with large high-voltage infrastructure,
the loss of scenic and aesthetic value, viewshed impacts from 200-foot steel lattice towers, and the
land-use restrictions imposed by the right-of-way itself. In Oncor Electric Delivery Co. v. Clack,
a Wichita County jury awarded a landowner approximately eight times Oncor' s initial
condemnation offer for a 345-kV line because the jury found the transmission infrastructure
diminished the value ofthe entire parcel, not merely the strip of land within the right-of-way. The
lines proposed here are 765-kV, with significantly larger towers, wider rights-of-way, greater
EMF, and far greater documented health, safety, and environmental impacts than the 345-kV line
at issue in Clack, so the property-value harm can reasonably be expected to exceed what the jury
recognized there.

   •   Are there alternative routes or configurations offacilities that would have a less negative
       e#ect on landowners, andwhatwould be the incremental cost of those routes or
       configurations?

Yes. A more direct alternative routing between the same endpoints, and the use of the existing
adjacent corridor, would each have a less negative effect on landowners and the environment than
the F43 to G43 segment, and would avoid the endangered-species crossing at Cobbs Springs
entirely. As to incremental cost, the comparison runs in the Frious' favor: because the F43 to G43
segment is the longer, less direct, and more expensive option, the alternatives reduce cost rather
than add it. The applicants, who bear the burden, have not quantified or justified the difference,
and have not demonstrated that the southernmost route is necessary and appropriate.

   Best Management Practices

   •   Are the standard best management practices adequate? If not, what additional practices
       should be required for the proposed transmission facilities?

For the F43 to G43 crossing of Cobbs Springs and Cobb Springs Branch, no standard construction
or operating best management practice can render the route compatible with the survival of the
endangered salamander populations, because the harms (fracturing of karst limestone, alteration
of the groundwater flow paths that feed the springs, contamination of pristine spring water,
removal of riparian vegetation, and recurring maintenance disturbance) flow from the construction
and permanent presence of the line itself. The appropriate practice is avoidance: route away from

Wildlife Department and consultation with the U. S. Fish and Wildlife Service under Section 7 of
the Endangered Species Act before any route decision affecting this habitat.

    Texas Parks and Wildlife Department
   •   Did the Texas Parks and Wildlife Department provide any recommendations or
       informational comments regarding this application in accordance with section
        12.0011(b) of the Texas Parks and Wildlife Code, andif so, how should the Commission
       respond through its order?

The dispositive point for the Frious is that the applicants did not properly coordinate with the Texas
Parks and Wildlife Department as required. A complete CCN application and a proper
environmental routing analysis require the applicants to coordinate with the Department, to request
its recommendations and informational comments under Texas Parks and Wildlife Code §
12.0011(b), and to document and address that coordination in the environmental assessment
supporting the application. To the Frious' knowledge, the record contains no evidence that the
applicants coordinated with the Department regarding the F43 to G43 segment's crossing of Cobbs
Springs and Cobb Springs Branch, the federally endangered Salado Salamander and Jollyville
Plateau salamander, or the U. S. Fish and Wildlife Service's designated critical habitat Unit 6. Nor
does the record document the consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service that Section 7
of the Endangered Species Act requires where a federal nexus exists.

That failure to coordinate goes to the heart of the environmental-integrity criterion under PURA §
37.056(c) and 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B), and it is a material deficiency in the application. The
Commission should respond through its order by, first, requiring the applicants to coordinate with
the Texas Parks and Wildlife Department and to place the Department' s recommendations and
informational comments in the record; second, requiring the applicants to document any
consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service under Section 7 of the Endangered Species
Act, both as to the listed species and as to designated critical habitat Unit 6; and third, declining to
approve any route using segments F43 or G43 until that coordination and consultation are complete
and have been scrutinized in this proceeding.
